profile.name: Ali Najafizadeh
profile.title: Lead Software Engineer
profile.tagline: I build distributed systems, and the tooling that keeps them workable for the teams who run them.
summary: Backend engineer who builds the things other engineers build on. Fourteen years of Go, spent on distributed systems, developer platforms, and the unglamorous plumbing (configuration, tracing, code generation, release tooling) that decides whether a team ships or stalls.

I gravitate to the problem nobody has scoped yet. A Rails monolith that has to become services without a maintenance window. A fleet of microservices with no way to see a request cross them. Every team writing the same bootstrap code a slightly different way. My pattern is the same each time: build the first version myself, prove it under real traffic, then turn it into the standard everyone actually wants to adopt.

Tech lead at Flipp, Brex, and Blockthrough, and now setting Go standards across 1Password. Comfortable with identity and access work, from OAuth2 and SSO to payment integrations. Remote and async by habit, and at my best when the problem is ambiguous and the fix has to survive contact with production.

highlights: Building 1Go, the internal SDK that every Go team at 1Password now starts from.
Putting configuration, logging, tracing, and service scaffolding behind one ergonomic API, so a new secure service begins with the basics already decided instead of rebuilt.
Setting the Go engineering standards the rest of the company builds against, and coaching teams toward idiomatic, production-grade patterns in a security-first environment.
Built a platform that lets any Coinbase developer take an end-to-end system from idea to deployment on internal infrastructure, without first becoming an expert in that infrastructure.
Designed the abstractions that absorb distributed-system complexity, the part teams most often get wrong, so product work stays product work.
Turned patterns that teams kept rewriting into supported tools and frameworks, shortening the path from a new repo to a shipped feature.
Built backend services for the carbon accounting platform that ingest and normalize large volumes of operational data.
Spent the five-month engagement on the two things that decide whether such a platform is trusted: pipeline reliability, and APIs that are hard to use incorrectly.
Worked shoulder to shoulder with a small, deeply technical team in a fast-moving climate-tech environment.
Led the team that made the open-source Prebid Server (Go) Blockthrough's own, extending its ad-tech capabilities and tuning it for our production traffic.
Owned btctl, the company CLI, and collapsed deployment and everyday engineering chores into one predictable tool.
Open-sourced a self-updating SDK and CLI that lets any Go binary update itself through GitHub Releases and Actions, so cutting a release stopped being a manual ritual.
Introduced distributed tracing at Blockthrough and Eye/o, taking OpenTelemetry from nothing to end-to-end visibility across microservices.
Wired Grafana and Tempo together so an engineer can follow a single request across services instead of reconstructing it from logs.
Worked out of the CTO office on developer experience for the whole engineering organization: find where the workflow or the tooling is quietly taxing everyone, then go fix it.
Built brexctl, the internal control CLI that gave engineers one command surface for day-to-day operations.
Built dynamic preview environments so a change could be exercised in a production-like setting before it went anywhere near production.
Architected integration plugins for several payment gateways, where correctness and secure handling are the entire job.
Contributed to the Temporal workflow engine used internally for durable workflows.
Led the breakup of a large Ruby on Rails monolith into modular services on a Kafka pipeline, which freed each team to pick the right language for its problem instead of inheriting one.

Designed one-click project scaffolding for Node.js, Ruby, Go, and Scala: repository, CircleCI configuration, staging and production environments all provisioned in a single step, so a new service started with the boring parts already done.
Built the shared pieces underneath that work, including a Go Avro/Kafka library for efficient serialization and Node.js streaming tools for real-time pipelines.
Key engineer through Alida's acquisition of Pressly Inc, responsible for integrating Alida's C#/.NET system with Pressly's Go backend.
Wrote the bridging tools that let two stacks built on different assumptions understand each other.
Wrote and ran the migration that moved data onto the merged system, keeping downtime short and the platform stable.
Led a zero-downtime migration off Ruby on Rails and MongoDB onto Go and PostgreSQL, keeping the product continuously available for customers throughout.
Bet on React Native early and shipped iOS and Android from a single codebase.
Made that app self-updating by combining Go and Go Mobile, so fixes reached both platforms automatically.
Designed a bi-directional messaging system on Netty (Java), using non-blocking I/O to hold high volumes of concurrent connections at low latency.
Led the front-end architecture on Backbone.js and built the in-house toolchain that compiled and bundled JavaScript for production, back when there was no standard answer for that.
Built software and libraries for set-top boxes shipped by major telecoms including Rogers and Telus, covering media streaming, device management, and remote connectivity.

projects.name: orc
projects.tagline: Durable workflow orchestrator for Go, backed by SQLite
projects.description: A lightweight, embeddable, durable workflow orchestrator. Write ordinary Go functions and orc checkpoints their inputs, step outputs, and completion to SQLite, so a crash resumes instead of losing work. Includes durable queues, inter-workflow messaging, cron scheduling, and a bundled web dashboard.

projects.name: ella
projects.tagline: A compiler that generates Go and TypeScript HTTP clients and servers
projects.description: A compiler shaped by 12+ years of building backends and APIs. From a small, readable schema IDL it emits Go and TypeScript code that reads like something a careful engineer wrote by hand. Covers six HTTP communication patterns, including SSE, file uploads, and binary streaming.

projects.name: bus
projects.description: A message bus with no external dependencies, so no Redis, Kafka, or RabbitMQ to operate. Persistent by default on append-only logs, with HTTP/SSE transport that any language can speak, pattern matching, request/reply, optional NaCl encryption, and automatic redelivery.

projects.name: flex
projects.tagline: A cell-based flexbox layout engine for the terminal
projects.description: A composable layout engine rendered with lipgloss v2 and ready to drop into Bubble Tea v2. Combines exact integer cell sizing with a declarative Fit / Fixed / Grow model and first-class text alignment, for terminal UIs that stay correct as they resize.

projects.name: sahar
projects.tagline: A declarative layout engine in Go
projects.description: A composable layout engine built on a clean multi-pass algorithm, with a Fit / Fixed / Grow sizing model and full alignment. The ergonomic foundation that flex grew out of.

projects.name: immuta
projects.description: A focused append-only log library for durable, ordered storage. It is the persistence layer underneath the bus message broker.

projects.name: jsonrpc
projects.tagline: JSON-RPC v2 over HTTP, TCP and UDP
projects.description: A fresh take on JSON-RPC v2 in Go with multi-transport support, built for service communication that stays simple and predictable.

projects.name: sqlite
projects.tagline: A set of ergonomic tools on top of the SQLite Go library
projects.description: A wrapper and toolchain around SQLite in Go, with pooling and helpers that make the common cases short. It is the storage layer for orc and the other ella.to projects.

projects.name: selfupdate.go
projects.tagline: Self-update toolchain for Go CLI programs
projects.description: A small SDK and CLI for updating Go binaries on top of GitHub Releases and Actions, so any Go application can keep itself current without a separate distribution story.

projects.name: microui
projects.tagline: A tiny immediate-mode UI library for Go
projects.description: A pure-Go immediate-mode UI library ported from rxi/microui, with no cgo and no dependencies. It is renderer-agnostic, emitting a list of draw commands each frame for any backend to draw, and ships built-in controls (windows, panels, buttons, sliders, textboxes, trees, popups) plus a ready-made terminal renderer.
